text: Land plants grew out of the green algae lineage about 500 million years ago; these sea greens are their distant cousins.
source: Leliaert et al. 2012, Critical Reviews in Plant Sciences 31:1-46 (doi:10.1080/07352689.2011.615705)

text: Ostreococcus, a sea green alga under a thousandth of a millimetre wide, is the smallest free-living cell with a nucleus known.
source: Courties et al. 1994, Nature 370:255 (doi:10.1038/370255a0)

text: Ostreococcus also has one of the smallest genomes of any free-living cell with a nucleus, packed into 20 tiny chromosomes.
Micromonas, a tiny sea green alga, also swallows bacteria, mixing sunlight and hunting to get by in poor water.
source: McKie-Krisberg and Sanders 2014, ISME Journal 8:1953-1961 (doi:10.1038/ismej.2014.16)

text: Green algae share chlorophyll b with land plants, which is why both wear the same leafy green.
source: Falkowski and Raven 2007, Aquatic Photosynthesis, 2nd ed., Princeton University Press

text: Many green algae ride out hard times as a thick-walled resting zygote that can wait in the mud until the water turns kind again.
source: Graham, Graham and Wilcox 2009, Algae, 2nd ed., Benjamin Cummings

text: Fossil resting cysts of prasinophyte green algae, called Tasmanites, are so packed in some shales that the rock burns as oil shale.
source: Tappan 1980, The Paleobiology of Plant Protists, W.H. Freeman

text: Alexandrium makes saxitoxin; mussels that filter it store the poison and can paralyse people who eat them (paralytic shellfish poisoning).
source: Anderson et al. 2012, Harmful Algae 14:10-35 (doi:10.1016/j.hal.2011.10.012)

text: Saxitoxin plugs the channels nerves use to fire; a few milligrams eaten in shellfish can kill an adult.
source: Wiese et al. 2010, Marine Drugs 8:2185-2211 (doi:10.3390/md8072185)

text: In the Gulf of Maine, counts of Alexandrium cysts in the seabed mud are used to forecast how big next year's toxic bloom may be.
source: Anderson et al. 2014, Deep-Sea Research II 103:6-26 (doi:10.1016/j.dsr2.2013.10.002)

text: Some Alexandrium strains glow when the water is stirred, each flash lasting about a tenth of a second.
source: Valiadi and Iglesias-Rodriguez 2013, Microorganisms 1:3-25 (doi:10.3390/microorganisms1010003)

text: Chains of Alexandrium swim faster than single cells, which may help them hold their depth against mixing.
source: Fraga, Gallager and Anderson 1989, in Red Tides: Biology, Environmental Science and Toxicology, Elsevier, pp. 281-284

text: Alexandrium leaks chemicals that burst other protists nearby, clearing away rivals and the grazers that would eat it.
source: Tillmann and John 2002, Marine Ecology Progress Series 230:47-58 (doi:10.3354/meps230047)

text: Dinophysis steals its chloroplasts third-hand: from a red ciliate, Mesodinium, that stole them from a cryptophyte alga.
source: Park et al. 2006, Aquatic Microbial Ecology 45:101-106 (doi:10.3354/ame045101)

text: Dinophysis does not swallow its prey; it pierces it with a thin tube and sucks out the insides, a way of eating called myzocytosis.
source: Park et al. 2006, Aquatic Microbial Ecology 45:101-106 (doi:10.3354/ame045101)

text: Dinophysis toxins, okadaic acid and its kin, cause diarrhetic shellfish poisoning in people who eat tainted mussels.
source: Reguera et al. 2012, Harmful Algae 14:87-106 (doi:10.1016/j.hal.2011.10.016)

text: Dinophysis was named in 1839 but could not be kept alive in the lab until 2006, when it was finally fed its ciliate prey.
source: Park et al. 2006, Aquatic Microbial Ecology 45:101-106 (doi:10.3354/ame045101)

text: Dinophysis can close shellfish farms at a few hundred cells per litre, far too few to tint the water.
source: Reguera et al. 2012, Harmful Algae 14:87-106 (doi:10.1016/j.hal.2011.10.016)

text: Some open-ocean relatives of Dinophysis keep tiny cyanobacteria in a chamber between their sail-like lists, probably as partners.
source: Foster, Carpenter and Bergman 2006, Journal of Phycology 42:453-463 (doi:10.1111/j.1529-8817.2006.00206.x)

text: Sea-going Ceratium were moved to the genus Tripos, three-footed, in 2013; the lake species kept the old name Ceratium.
source: Gomez 2013, CICIMAR Oceanides 28:1-22 (doi:10.37543/oceanides.v28i1.119)

text: In warm seas Tripos often grows longer, more branched horns, thought to slow its sinking in warm water, which is thinner.
source: Smayda 1970, Oceanography and Marine Biology Annual Review 8:353-414

text: Tripos furca is a plant and a predator: it photosynthesises but also catches small ciliates, more so when nutrients run low.
source: Smalley, Coats and Stoecker 2003, Marine Ecology Progress Series 262:137-151 (doi:10.3354/meps262137)

text: In 1976 a vast Tripos bloom off New Jersey rotted and stripped the bottom water of oxygen, killing clams, lobsters and fish.
source: Swanson and Sindermann (eds) 1979, Oxygen depletion and associated benthic mortalities in New York Bight, 1976, NOAA Professional Paper 11

text: With its horns a Tripos cell can span a third of a millimetre, a giant beside cyanobacteria hundreds of times smaller.
source: Tomas (ed) 1997, Identifying Marine Phytoplankton, Academic Press

text: Some Tripos species link up into short chains of a few cells that swim as one.
source: Tomas (ed) 1997, Identifying Marine Phytoplankton, Academic Press

text: Unlike most dinoflagellates, Prorocentrum has no groove round its middle; both its flagella spring from its front end.
source: Taylor (ed) 1987, The Biology of Dinoflagellates, Blackwell

text: Its armour is just two plates, left and right, joined at a seam like the shell of a tiny clam.
source: Taylor (ed) 1987, The Biology of Dinoflagellates, Blackwell

text: Prorocentrum minimum has spread along coasts worldwide, blooming in water enriched by farm and city runoff.
source: Heil, Glibert and Fan 2005, Harmful Algae 4:449-470 (doi:10.1016/j.hal.2004.08.003)

text: Its cousin Prorocentrum lima lives on seaweed and sand rather than in open water, and makes the same toxins as Dinophysis.
source: Faust and Gulledge 2002, Contributions from the US National Herbarium 42:1-144

text: In Chesapeake Bay, spring blooms of Prorocentrum turn the water red-brown, a sight known as a mahogany tide.
source: Tango et al. 2005, Harmful Algae 4:525-531 (doi:10.1016/j.hal.2004.08.014)

text: Prorocentrum minimum does not live on light alone; it has been seen eating small cryptophyte algae.
source: Stoecker et al. 1997, Marine Ecology Progress Series 152:1-12 (doi:10.3354/meps152001)

text: A diatom lives in a glass box of two halves that fit like a pillbox and its lid, made of silica, the stuff of opal.
source: Round, Crawford and Mann 1990, The Diatoms, Cambridge University Press

text: Each daughter keeps one old half and builds a smaller one inside it, so diatoms shrink as they divide until sex restores their size.
source: Round, Crawford and Mann 1990, The Diatoms, Cambridge University Press

text: The barbed spines of some Chaetoceros lodge in fish gills; blooms of them have killed penned salmon in British Columbia.
source: Albright, Yang and Johnson 1993, Aquaculture 117:215-225 (doi:10.1016/0044-8486(93)90321-O)

text: After a bloom Chaetoceros cells turn into heavy resting spores; in the North Atlantic they carry much of the sinking carbon down.
source: Rynearson et al. 2013, Deep-Sea Research I 82:60-71 (doi:10.1016/j.dsr.2013.07.013)

text: The first diatom genome, read in 2004 from the centric Thalassiosira, showed it has a urea cycle, once thought to be only animal.
source: Armbrust et al. 2004, Science 306:79-86 (doi:10.1126/science.1101156)

text: A centric diatom is mostly a big sap-filled vacuole, which stores nitrate and lets the cell grow large cheaply.
source: Falkowski and Raven 2007, Aquatic Photosynthesis, 2nd ed., Princeton University Press

text: Coscinodiscus wailesii, a centric diatom, can reach half a millimetre across, almost big enough to see by eye.
source: Tomas (ed) 1997, Identifying Marine Phytoplankton, Academic Press

text: Pennate means feather-like: these diatoms are long boats whose glass markings run out from a midline like the barbs of a feather.
source: Round, Crawford and Mann 1990, The Diatoms, Cambridge University Press

text: On sand or mud, many pennate diatoms glide by pushing sticky threads out through a slit in their glass, the raphe.
source: Round, Crawford and Mann 1990, The Diatoms, Cambridge University Press

text: In 1987 mussels from Prince Edward Island poisoned over 100 people; the cause was domoic acid from the pennate diatom Pseudo-nitzschia.
source: Bates et al. 1989, Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences 46:1203-1215 (doi:10.1139/f89-156)

text: Crazed seabirds struck a California town in 1961, which Hitchcock read of while making The Birds; Pseudo-nitzschia toxin is the likely cause.
source: Bargu et al. 2012, Nature Geoscience 5:2-3 (doi:10.1038/ngeo1360)

text: Pennate diatoms living inside polar sea ice stain its underside brown and feed krill through the winter.
source: Arrigo 2014, Annual Review of Marine Science 6:439-467 (doi:10.1146/annurev-marine-010213-135103)

text: Asterionellopsis links its cells foot to foot into stars and spirals that drift in the surf of sandy beaches.
source: Round, Crawford and Mann 1990, The Diatoms, Cambridge University Press

text: Each coccolithophore builds an intricate coccosphere: chalk scales made one at a time inside the cell, then pushed out to tile its surface.
source: Taylor, Brownlee and Wheeler 2017, Annual Review of Marine Science 9:283-310 (doi:10.1146/annurev-marine-122414-034032)

text: The White Cliffs of Dover are chalk made largely of coccoliths that settled on a sea floor some 70 to 100 million years ago.
source: Tyrrell and Young 2009, Coccolithophores, in Encyclopedia of Ocean Sciences, 2nd ed., Academic Press, pp. 606-614

text: Carbon in coccolithophore fats buried in deep-sea mud shows that air CO2 fell sharply between about 45 and 25 million years ago.
source: Pagani et al. 2005, Science 309:600-603 (doi:10.1126/science.1110063)

text: Coccolithophores make fats called alkenones whose make-up shifts with water warmth; read in old mud, they give past sea temperatures.
Emiliania huxleyi blooms can spread over 100,000 square kilometres, so milky turquoise that they are seen from space.
source: Holligan et al. 1993, Global Biogeochemical Cycles 7:879-900 (doi:10.1029/93GB01731)

text: Plankton such as coccolithophores release a sulphur gas, part of the smell of the sea, which in air can help seed clouds.
Viruses end many Emiliania huxleyi blooms, bursting the cells and shedding clouds of loose chalk plates.
source: Bratbak, Egge and Heldal 1993, Marine Ecology Progress Series 93:39-48 (doi:10.3354/meps093039)

text: Emiliania huxleyi honours Cesare Emiliani, a founder of palaeoceanography, and Thomas Huxley, who named coccoliths in 1858.
In lab tests, water made more acidic by extra carbon dioxide led some coccolithophores to build thinner, malformed plates.
Cryptophytes swallowed a red alga long ago and still keep a shrunken leftover of its nucleus, the nucleomorph: a cell within a cell.
They catch green or orange light with phycobilin pigments, the same family that tints cyanobacteria, so they do well in dim water.
source: Kirk 2011, Light and Photosynthesis in Aquatic Ecosystems, 3rd ed., Cambridge University Press

text: Cryptophytes carry coiled ribbons called ejectisomes that spring out when disturbed, jolting the cell away in a zigzag escape.
source: Graham, Graham and Wilcox 2009, Algae, 2nd ed., Benjamin Cummings

text: A red ciliate, Mesodinium, steals cryptophyte chloroplasts and even their nuclei; its blooms can turn coastal water red.
source: Johnson et al. 2007, Nature 445:426-428 (doi:10.1038/nature05496)

text: Rich in healthy fats, cryptophytes are fine food for copepods and are grown on fish and shellfish farms to feed the young.
Cryptophyte means hidden plant: they are small and so fragile they burst when preserved, so they were long overlooked.
source: Graham, Graham and Wilcox 2009, Algae, 2nd ed., Benjamin Cummings

text: Cyanobacteria were the first to split water with sunlight; their oxygen began to build up in the air about 2.4 billion years ago.
source: Lyons, Reinhard and Planavsky 2014, Nature 506:307-315 (doi:10.1038/nature13068)

text: Stromatolites, layered rocks built by microbial mats, are among the oldest signs of life; cyanobacterial ones still grow in Shark Bay, Australia.
source: Allwood et al. 2006, Nature 441:714-718 (doi:10.1038/nature04764)

text: Almost every chloroplast in algae and plants descends from a cyanobacterium swallowed by another cell well over a billion years ago.
source: Archibald 2015, Current Biology 25:R911-R921 (doi:10.1016/j.cub.2015.07.055)

text: Prochlorococcus is the most abundant photosynthetic life on Earth: about three billion billion billion cells.
Prochlorococcus was discovered only in 1988, though it lives in nearly every sunlit drop of the warm open ocean.
Prochlorococcus splits into high-light strains near the surface and low-light strains deeper down, each in its own layer.
source: Moore, Rocap and Chisholm 1998, Nature 393:464-467 (doi:10.1038/30965)

text: Some Synechococcus swim with no flagellum at all, by a means still not fully understood; this was discovered only in 1985.
source: Waterbury et al. 1985, Science 230:74-76 (doi:10.1126/science.230.4721.74)

text: Trichodesmium fixes nitrogen gas by day, though oxygen from its own photosynthesis spoils the enzyme, by setting some cells apart for it.
source: Berman-Frank et al. 2001, Science 294:1534-1537 (doi:10.1126/science.1064082)

text: Darwin saw Trichodesmium off Brazil from the Beagle in 1832; he noted that Cook's sailors had called it sea sawdust.
source: Darwin 1845, Journal of Researches (Voyage of the Beagle), 2nd ed., John Murray, ch. 1

text: The Red Sea may owe its name to Trichodesmium erythraeum, whose blooms can tint the water red-brown.
source: Darwin 1845, Journal of Researches (Voyage of the Beagle), 2nd ed., John Murray, ch. 1 (as told by M.J. Berkeley)

text: In warm, nutrient-poor seas Trichodesmium is a major source of new nitrogen, fertilising the water for other life.
Its colonies come as puffs and tufts, and gas vesicles inside the filaments float them up toward the light.
source: Walsby 1994, Microbiological Reviews 58:94-144 (doi:10.1128/mr.58.1.94-144.1994)

text: Trichodesmium puffs grab desert dust that falls on the sea and roll it to their centre to mine the iron they need.
source: Rubin, Berman-Frank and Shaked 2011, Nature Geoscience 4:529-534 (doi:10.1038/ngeo1181)

text: By day colonies store heavy sugar and may sink; burning it lets them float up again, a slow daily ride up and down.
source: Villareal and Carpenter 2003, Microbial Ecology 45:1-10 (doi:10.1007/s00248-002-1012-5)

text: Diatoms do about a fifth of all photosynthesis on Earth, roughly as much as all the world's rainforests.
source: Armbrust 2009, Nature 459:185-192 (doi:10.1038/nature08057)

text: Alfred Nobel soaked nitroglycerine into kieselguhr, earth made of fossil diatom glass, to make dynamite safe to carry.
source: Round, Crawford and Mann 1990, The Diatoms, Cambridge University Press

text: When scientists added iron to the equatorial Pacific in 1995, diatoms bloomed and chlorophyll rose up to 27 times.
Dust from the Bodele, a dry Saharan lakebed of fossil diatoms, blows across the Atlantic and helps fertilise the Amazon.
source: Koren et al. 2006, Environmental Research Letters 1:014005 (doi:10.1088/1748-9326/1/1/014005)

text: Diatom glass is pierced by pores so regular that microscope makers once used diatoms to test the sharpness of their lenses.
source: Round, Crawford and Mann 1990, The Diatoms, Cambridge University Press

text: Diatoms reuse silica over and over: only about 3% of the glass they make each year ends up buried in the seabed.
source: Treguer et al. 1995, Science 268:375-379 (doi:10.1126/science.268.5209.375)

text: Red tides are often dense dinoflagellate blooms, but they can also be brown, green or orange, and many are harmless.
source: Anderson, Cembella and Hallegraeff 2012, Annual Review of Marine Science 4:143-176 (doi:10.1146/annurev-marine-120308-081121)

text: Their glow may be a burglar alarm: a flash lights up the grazer eating the cell, drawing in fish that eat the grazer.
source: Abrahams and Townsend 1993, Ecology 74:258-260 (doi:10.2307/1939521)

text: Some dinoflagellates hold dozens of times more DNA than a human cell, in chromosomes that stay tightly coiled all the time.
source: Hackett et al. 2004, American Journal of Botany 91:1523-1534 (doi:10.3732/ajb.91.10.1523)

text: About half of all dinoflagellates have no chloroplasts and live as hunters, more like tiny animals than plants.
source: Jeong et al. 2010, Ocean Science Journal 45:65-91 (doi:10.1007/s12601-010-0007-2)

text: The algae that feed reef corals from inside their tissues are dinoflagellates; losing them is what turns corals white in bleaching.
source: LaJeunesse et al. 2018, Current Biology 28:2570-2580 (doi:10.1016/j.cub.2018.07.008)

text: Dinoflagellate means whirling whip: one flagellum lies in a groove round the cell and spins it as it swims.
source: Taylor (ed) 1987, The Biology of Dinoflagellates, Blackwell

text: Some dinoflagellates swim down at night to take up nutrients at depth and back up by day to the light, metres each way.
source: Eppley, Holm-Hansen and Strickland 1968, Journal of Phycology 4:333-340 (doi:10.1111/j.1529-8817.1968.tb04704.x)

text: Phytoplankton are under 1% of the world's plant mass, yet they do about half of all the photosynthesis on Earth.
Plankton make about half the oxygen produced each year, but sea life uses nearly all of it again; the air's vast store changes very slowly.
Without the plankton's biological pump, carbon dioxide in the air would be roughly 200 parts per million higher than it is.
source: Volk and Hoffert 1985, in Sundquist and Broecker (eds), The Carbon Cycle and Atmospheric CO2, AGU Geophysical Monograph 32:99-110 (doi:10.1029/GM032p0099)

text: The ocean's whole stock of phytoplankton is eaten and regrown about once a week; a forest takes decades.
Upwelling coasts, a tiny share of the ocean, were once estimated to yield about half the world's fish catch.
Satellites have mapped the green of ocean chlorophyll from space since 1978, watching blooms come and go across the planet.
source: McClain 2009, Annual Review of Marine Science 1:19-42 (doi:10.1146/annurev.marine.010908.163650)

text: Most of the world's oil formed from plankton, largely algae, buried in seabed mud and slowly cooked over millions of years.
source: Tissot and Welte 1984, Petroleum Formation and Occurrence, 2nd ed., Springer

text: A 1934 rule of thumb for microbes is still debated: everything is everywhere, but the environment selects.
source: de Wit and Bouvier 2006, Environmental Microbiology 8:755-758 (doi:10.1111/j.1462-2920.2006.01017.x)

text: Sunlight fades fast in the sea: in clear ocean about 1% is left near 150 m, in murky coastal water within a few metres.
source: Kirk 2011, Light and Photosynthesis in Aquatic Ecosystems, 3rd ed., Cambridge University Press

text: Water swallows red light within the top ten metres or so, so the depths look blue and red animals look black there.
source: Kirk 2011, Light and Photosynthesis in Aquatic Ecosystems, 3rd ed., Cambridge University Press

text: Many seas hide a deep chlorophyll maximum, where cells meet nutrients from below in dim light and pack in more chlorophyll.
source: Cullen 2015, Annual Review of Marine Science 7:207-239 (doi:10.1146/annurev-marine-010213-135111)

text: A spring bloom starts, Sverdrup argued in 1953, once the mixed layer is shallow enough that cells gain more from light than they lose.
source: Sverdrup 1953, Journal du Conseil International pour l'Exploration de la Mer 18:287-295

text: A thermocline, where warm water lies on cold, works like a lid: mixing across it is weak, so the nutrients below stay out of reach.
source: Mann and Lazier 2006, Dynamics of Marine Ecosystems, 3rd ed., Blackwell

text: Each dusk zooplankton and small fish rise from the depths to feed and sink again at dawn, the largest daily migration on Earth.
Shelf seas are layered like a sandwich in summer: a warm surface layer, a thermocline, and a cold bottom layer stirred by the tide.
source: Simpson and Sharples 2012, Introduction to the Physical and Biological Oceanography of Shelf Seas, Cambridge University Press

text: Plankton hold carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus in a near-fixed ratio of 106 to 16 to 1, and so does deep water: Redfield's ratio.
source: Redfield 1958, American Scientist 46:205-221

text: Viruses burst cells and spill them back into the water, the viral shunt, keeping nutrients near the surface for other cells.
source: Wilhelm and Suttle 1999, BioScience 49:781-788 (doi:10.2307/1313569)

text: Vast seas hold plenty of nitrate but little life; John Martin argued in the late 1980s that iron is what is missing there.
source: Martin 1990, Paleoceanography 5:1-13 (doi:10.1029/PA005i001p00001)

text: In most of the sunlit ocean nitrogen runs out first and limits growth; phosphorus and iron limit it in some regions.
source: Moore et al. 2013, Nature Geoscience 6:701-710 (doi:10.1038/ngeo1765)

text: Silica in the sea comes mostly from rock weathered on land and carried by rivers, and diatoms are its main users.
source: Treguer and De La Rocha 2013, Annual Review of Marine Science 5:477-501 (doi:10.1146/annurev-marine-121211-172346)

text: Dead diatom glass dissolves slowly, so silica returns to the water much later than nitrogen, which bacteria free within days.
source: Treguer and De La Rocha 2013, Annual Review of Marine Science 5:477-501 (doi:10.1146/annurev-marine-121211-172346)

text: Where winds push surface water away from a coast, cold deep water wells up in its place, bringing nutrients to the light.
source: Mann and Lazier 2006, Dynamics of Marine Ecosystems, 3rd ed., Blackwell

text: The sea's top film, under a millimetre thick, is a habitat of its own, the surface microlayer, rich in fatty gels, bacteria and viruses.
source: Cunliffe et al. 2013, Progress in Oceanography 109:104-116 (doi:10.1016/j.pocean.2012.08.004)

text: Underwater, light rain is a high ringing of tiny bubbles trapped by drops, near 15 kHz; hydrophones can measure rainfall by it.
source: Medwin et al. 1992, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 92:1613-1623 (doi:10.1121/1.403902)

text: Gases cross the sea surface much faster in wind; breaking waves and bubbles speed the exchange many times over.
source: Wanninkhof 1992, Journal of Geophysical Research 97:7373-7382 (doi:10.1029/92JC00188)

text: Seen from below, the whole sky squeezes into a bright circle overhead, Snell's window; beyond it the surface is a mirror.
source: Lynch and Livingston 2001, Color and Light in Nature, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press

text: Wind can roll the surface layer into long spinning cells that gather foam, weed and scum into lines called windrows.
The ocean takes up about a quarter of the carbon dioxide people release each year, nearly all of it through the surface.
source: Friedlingstein et al. 2022, Earth System Science Data 14:4811-4900 (doi:10.5194/essd-14-4811-2022)

text: Marine snow, flakes of dead cells, mucus and fecal pellets, falls through the sea all the time and can take weeks to reach the deep floor.
source: Alldredge and Silver 1988, Progress in Oceanography 20:41-82 (doi:10.1016/0079-6611(88)90053-5)

text: Less than 1% of the carbon fixed at the surface ends up buried in seabed mud, but over the ages that buried carbon became oil and gas.
source: Hedges and Keil 1995, Marine Chemistry 49:81-115 (doi:10.1016/0304-4203(95)00008-F)

text: Dinoflagellate cysts buried about a century in a Swedish fjord were woken and grew: seabed mud holds a living seed bank.
source: Ribeiro et al. 2011, Nature Communications 2:311 (doi:10.1038/ncomms1314); Lundholm et al. 2011, Phycologia 50:629-640 (doi:10.2216/11-16.1)

text: Resting cells of the diatom Skeletonema, asleep for up to a century in Danish fjord mud, have been revived and grown again.
Beggiatoa mats look white because each filament is packed with globules of sulphur, made as it feeds on hydrogen sulphide.
source: Jorgensen and Nelson 2004, Geological Society of America Special Paper 379:63-81

text: In seabed mud, cable bacteria form living wires centimetres long that carry electric current from deep mud to oxygen above.
source: Pfeffer et al. 2012, Nature 491:218-221 (doi:10.1038/nature11586)

text: Bait left on the deep seabed draws swarms of scavenging amphipods within hours, sometimes minutes.
source: Jamieson et al. 2010, Trends in Ecology and Evolution 25:190-197 (doi:10.1016/j.tree.2009.09.009)

text: Ostracods, seed shrimps in a two-part shell, have left fossils for about 450 million years; some sea species glow blue.
source: Horne, Cohen and Martens 2002, The Ostracoda: Applications in Quaternary Research, AGU Geophysical Monograph 131:5-36

text: The deep-sea isopod Bathynomus, a cousin of the garden woodlouse, can grow longer than 40 cm.
source: Lowry and Dempsey 2006, Memoires du Museum national d'Histoire naturelle 193:163-192

text: About half of the deep seafloor is carpeted in chalky ooze, made mostly of coccoliths and the shells of forams.
source: Seibold and Berger 1996, The Sea Floor, 3rd ed., Springer

text: Over 400 coastal dead zones have been reported, covering more than 245,000 square km, mostly fed by fertiliser runoff and fossil fuel burning.
source: Diaz and Rosenberg 2008, Science 321:926-929 (doi:10.1126/science.1156401)

text: Each summer Mississippi nutrients feed blooms whose rot leaves a dead zone off Louisiana, often near 15,000 square kilometres.
source: Rabalais, Turner and Wiseman 2002, Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics 33:235-263 (doi:10.1146/annurev.ecolsys.33.010802.150513)

text: Below roughly 100 to 200 m the Black Sea holds no oxygen, only hydrogen sulphide; it is the largest such basin on Earth.
As oxygen falls, crabs and fish flee and worms leave their burrows; below about 2 mL per litre many begin to die.
source: Diaz and Rosenberg 1995, Oceanography and Marine Biology Annual Review 33:245-303

text: Spring tides, the biggest, come at new and full moon when Sun and Moon pull in line; neaps come at half moon.
source: Pugh and Woodworth 2014, Sea-Level Science, Cambridge University Press

text: Where tidal currents are strong a shelf sea stays mixed all summer; a front divides it from layered water, often rich in plankton.
source: Simpson and Hunter 1974, Nature 250:404-406 (doi:10.1038/250404a0)

text: The Bay of Fundy in Canada has the largest tides on Earth, rising and falling as much as about 16 m.
source: Pugh and Woodworth 2014, Sea-Level Science, Cambridge University Press

text: Tidal friction, much of it on shallow shelves, slowly lengthens Earth's day; the Moon drifts about 3.8 cm farther away each year.
High tide comes about 50 minutes later each day, because the Moon takes 24 hours 50 minutes to come round overhead again.
source: Pugh and Woodworth 2014, Sea-Level Science, Cambridge University Press

text: In the dark Arctic winter, zooplankton migrate by moonlight, sinking deeper around each full moon across the whole Arctic.
source: Last et al. 2016, Current Biology 26:244-251 (doi:10.1016/j.cub.2015.11.038)

text: Milky seas, glowing for nights over thousands of square kilometres, have been seen by satellite; glowing bacteria are thought to cause them.
In Puerto Rico's bioluminescent bays the dinoflagellate Pyrodinium is so dense that every paddle stroke leaves a blue-green trail.
source: Soler-Figueroa and Otero 2015, Estuaries and Coasts 38:84-92 (doi:10.1007/s12237-014-9827-0)

text: About three quarters of the animals filmed in the water column off California can make their own light.
source: Martini and Haddock 2017, Scientific Reports 7:45750 (doi:10.1038/srep45750)

text: Prochlorococcus cells in the open ocean divide in step, mostly at night, timed by the daily cycle of light.
A millilitre of seawater holds about ten million viruses, the most numerous biological things in the sea.
Viruses are thought to kill about a fifth of the ocean's microbial biomass every day.
source: Suttle 2007, Nature Reviews Microbiology 5:801-812 (doi:10.1038/nrmicro1750)

text: The sea holds about 10 to the 30 viruses; laid end to end they would stretch farther than the nearest galaxies.
Viruses of cyanobacteria carry their own photosynthesis genes, keeping a dying host harvesting light to build more viruses.
Some ocean viruses have viruses of their own: a virophage that can only multiply by hijacking a giant virus inside its host.
source: Fischer and Suttle 2011, Science 332:231-234 (doi:10.1126/science.1199412)

text: A virus spreads fastest where its host is crowded, so viruses tend to kill the winner and help rare species persist.
source: Thingstad 2000, Limnology and Oceanography 45:1320-1328 (doi:10.4319/lo.2000.45.6.1320)

text: Copepods, crustaceans the size of a rice grain or smaller, may be the most numerous animals on Earth.
Single-celled grazers, such as ciliates and small dinoflagellates, eat about two thirds of the plankton's daily growth.
source: Calbet and Landry 2004, Limnology and Oceanography 49:51-57 (doi:10.4319/lo.2004.49.1.0051)

text: Antarctic krill weigh in at roughly 380 million tonnes, one of the largest masses of any wild animal species.
source: Atkinson, Siegel, Pakhomov, Jessopp and Loeb 2009, Deep-Sea Research I 56:727-740 (doi:10.1016/j.dsr.2008.12.007)

text: A startled copepod can jump hundreds of body lengths per second, among the fastest escapes of any animal for its size.
source: Kiorboe, Andersen, Langlois and Jakobsen 2010, Journal of the Royal Society Interface 7:1591-1602 (doi:10.1098/rsif.2010.0176)

text: Krill swarms grazing a bloom make fecal pellets that sink fast, carrying carbon to the deep.
source: Belcher et al. 2019, Nature Communications 10:889 (doi:10.1038/s41467-019-08847-1)

text: Tintinnid ciliates build vase-shaped houses called loricae, some studded with grains or coccoliths they glue on.
source: Dolan, Montagnes, Agatha, Coats and Stoecker (eds) 2013, The Biology and Ecology of Tintinnid Ciliates, Wiley-Blackwell

text: In winter Calanus copepods rest hundreds of metres down, living on an oil sac they filled during the spring bloom.
source: Falk-Petersen et al. 2009, Marine Biology Research 5:18-39 (doi:10.1080/17451000802512267)

text: Each winter the KwaZulu-Natal sardine run sends shoals kilometres long up the South African coast, trailed by dolphins, sharks and gannets.
source: Freon et al. 2010, African Journal of Marine Science 32:449-479 (doi:10.2989/1814232X.2010.519451)

text: Sardines can switch: they filter small plankton with fine gill rakers, or snap up larger prey one by one.
source: van der Lingen 1994, Marine Ecology Progress Series 109:1-13 (doi:10.3354/meps109001)

text: Pacific sardines and anchovies take turns booming for decades at a time, swinging with the climate of the ocean.
source: Chavez et al. 2003, Science 299:217-221 (doi:10.1126/science.1075880)

text: The California sardine fishery of Steinbeck's Cannery Row collapsed in the late 1940s, from heavy fishing and a cooler ocean.
source: Radovich 1982, CalCOFI Reports 23:56-78

text: Sardine flanks shine with stacked guanine crystals that act as mirrors, hiding the fish against the water when seen from the side.
source: Denton 1970, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 258:285-313 (doi:10.1098/rstb.1970.0037)

text: A solitary salp buds off chains of clones, and the chain members breed sexually to make solitary salps again.
source: Henschke, Everett, Richardson and Suthers 2016, Trends in Ecology and Evolution 31:720-733 (doi:10.1016/j.tree.2016.06.007)

text: Salp fecal pellets are dense and can sink over a kilometre a day, a fast lane for carbon to the deep.
source: Bruland and Silver 1981, Marine Biology 63:295-300 (doi:10.1007/BF00395999)

text: Salps look like jellies but are tunicates, among the closest living relatives of animals with backbones, us included.
source: Delsuc et al. 2006, Nature 439:965-968 (doi:10.1038/nature04336)

text: Salp numbers can explode when food is plentiful, budding faster than their predators can eat them.
source: Henschke, Everett, Richardson and Suthers 2016, Trends in Ecology and Evolution 31:720-733 (doi:10.1016/j.tree.2016.06.007)

text: A salp swims by jet: muscle bands squeeze its barrel and push water out the back, and the same flow feeds it.
source: Bone (ed) 1998, The Biology of Pelagic Tunicates, Oxford University Press

text: The heaviest bony fish on record is a Mola alexandrini sunfish of about 2,700 kg, found off the Azores in 2021.
source: Gomes-Pereira et al. 2023, Journal of Fish Biology 102:290-293 (doi:10.1111/jfb.15244)

text: One sunfish was estimated to carry 300 million eggs, more than any other known animal with a backbone.
Sunfish dive into cold depths to hunt jellies and siphonophores, then rest at the surface to warm up again.
source: Nakamura, Goto and Sato 2015, Journal of Animal Ecology 84:590-603 (doi:10.1111/1365-2656.12346)

text: Basking at the surface, sunfish let seabirds such as albatrosses pick parasites off their skin.
A sunfish has no true tail: its rear fin, the clavus, is formed from elements of its dorsal and anal fins.
source: Johnson and Britz 2005, Journal of Morphology 266:11-21 (doi:10.1002/jmor.10242)

text: A moon jelly starts as a polyp on rock that splits into a stack of baby jellies, which pop off one by one.
The four pale rings that give the moon jelly its name are its gonads, seen through the clear bell.
Moon jellies bear low oxygen far better than fish, so they can live and feed in dead-zone water that fish avoid.
source: Purcell et al. 2001, in Rabalais and Turner (eds), Coastal Hypoxia, AGU Coastal and Estuarine Studies 58:77-100 (doi:10.1029/CE058p0077)

text: Swarms of moon jellies have clogged the cooling-water intakes of power stations and shut them down.
source: Purcell, Uye and Lo 2007, Marine Ecology Progress Series 350:153-174 (doi:10.3354/meps07093)

text: A moon jelly is over 95% water and has no brain or heart; a net of nerves runs the pulsing of its bell.
The rainbows rippling along a comb jelly are light scattered by its beating combs; its own glow, when it has one, is blue or green.
source: Haddock and Case 1999, Marine Biology 133:571-582 (doi:10.1007/s002270050497)

text: Comb jellies are the largest animals that swim with cilia, the tiny beating hairs that also move single cells.
source: Tamm 2014, Invertebrate Biology 133:1-46 (doi:10.1111/ivb.12042)

text: In the 1980s the comb jelly Mnemiopsis, carried in ships' ballast water, overran the Black Sea and helped crash its anchovy fishery.
source: Shiganova 1998, Fisheries Oceanography 7:305-310 (doi:10.1046/j.1365-2419.1998.00080.x)

text: Gene order evidence from 2023 suggests comb jellies branched off before every other animal, even sponges.
The comb jelly Beroe hunts other comb jellies and can swallow prey nearly its own size whole.
source: Tamm 2014, Invertebrate Biology 133:1-46 (doi:10.1111/ivb.12042)

text: Mnemiopsis has an anus that appears only when needed, opening about once an hour and then vanishing again.
source: Tamm 2019, Invertebrate Biology 138:3-16 (doi:10.1111/ivb.12236)

text: A diatom's lattice of glass pores bends light like a photonic crystal: why their rims shimmer.
source: Fuhrmann et al. 2004, Applied Physics B 78:257-260 (doi:10.1007/s00340-004-1419-4)

text: Copepods graze long diatom chains several times faster than single cells, so some diatoms shorten their chains when copepods are near.
source: Bergkvist et al. 2012, Limnology and Oceanography 57:318-324 (doi:10.4319/lo.2012.57.1.0318)

text: Margalef's mandala: diatoms rule stirred, rich water; dinoflagellates rule calm, layered water.
source: Margalef 1978, Oceanologica Acta 1:493-509

text: Dinoflagellates glow on a daily clock: kept in constant dim light, Gonyaulax still glows most at the hours of its old night.
source: Hastings and Sweeney 1958, Biological Bulletin 115:440-458 (doi:10.2307/1539108)

text: Sardines filter phytoplankton as well as zooplankton: off Portugal, diatoms and dinoflagellates are a big part of their diet.
source: Garrido et al. 2008, Marine Ecology Progress Series 354:245-256 (doi:10.3354/meps07201)

text: River water is lighter than seawater, so a lens of fresh water can float on the sea and seal off the water below.
source: Simpson and Sharples 2012, Introduction to the Physical and Biological Oceanography of Shelf Seas, Cambridge University Press

text: In winter the surface cools until it is as heavy as the water beneath, and the whole column turns over. Nutrients that gathered near the seabed all summer are stirred back up toward the light.
source: Simpson and Sharples 2012, Introduction to the Physical and Biological Oceanography of Shelf Seas, Cambridge University Press

text: Diatoms lead in winter because the stirring that tumbles cells through the dark costs them nothing: they cannot swim anyway, and they grow whenever mixing carries them up into the light.
source: Margalef 1978, Oceanologica Acta 1:493-509

text: Winter water is rich but dark: nutrients are plentiful after the mixing, but the days are short, the sun is low and cells are stirred deep, so most growth waits for spring.
source: Sverdrup 1953, Journal du Conseil 18:287-295

text: In spring the days lengthen and the sun climbs. Once the surface warms enough to stop mixing so deep, cells stay in the light long enough to grow faster than they are lost, and the year's first big bloom can start.
source: Sverdrup 1953, Journal du Conseil 18:287-295

text: Diatoms usually win the spring bloom: the winter mixing has left plenty of silica for their glass walls, and they do not mind the stirring that still churns the young spring water.
source: Egge and Aksnes 1992, Marine Ecology Progress Series 83:281-289

text: A diatom bloom can strip the surface of silica, which only diatoms need. When it runs short, their growth stalls and other algae take the water.
source: Egge and Aksnes 1992, Marine Ecology Progress Series 83:281-289

text: In summer the sun warms the surface into a light layer floating on cold bottom water. The boundary, the thermocline, is so stable that the wind barely mixes across it, so the nutrients below stay out of reach of the sunlit cells above.
source: Simpson and Sharples 2012, Introduction to the Physical and Biological Oceanography of Shelf Seas, Cambridge University Press

text: In layered summer water the best place to live is often just above the thermocline, where a little light meets nutrients leaking up from below. Many cells gather there in a chlorophyll layer hidden beneath the surface.
source: Cullen 2015, Annual Review of Marine Science 7:207-239

text: Dinoflagellates bloom in calm, layered water. Turbulence upsets their swimming and their cell division, so storms favour diatoms and calm favours them.
source: Margalef 1978, Oceanologica Acta 1:493-509

text: Summer belongs to swimmers: with the surface stripped of nutrients, dinoflagellates that can swim down toward the nutrients and back up to the light have the edge over cells that just drift.
source: Smayda and Reynolds 2001, Journal of Plankton Research 23:447-461

text: Many dinoflagellates swim down at night toward the richer water below and rise again at dawn to photosynthesise: a daily commute between light above and nutrients below.
source: Eppley, Holm-Hansen and Strickland 1968, Journal of Phycology 4:333-340

text: Phytoplankton cannot photosynthesise in the dark. At night they live on what they stored by day and slow their metabolism down, on a daily clock of their own.
source: Falkowski and Raven 2007, Aquatic Photosynthesis, Princeton University Press

text: A storm churns the surface layer deeper and mixes nutrient-rich water up from below. Diatoms ride out the churn; dinoflagellates struggle in it.
source: Margalef 1978, Oceanologica Acta 1:493-509

text: In autumn the surface cools and the storms return, breaking up the summer layers. Nutrients mixed up from below often feed a second, smaller bloom before the dark of winter.
source: Longhurst 2007, Ecological Geography of the Sea, Academic Press

text: A dead zone is a bloom's afterlife: dead cells sink and bacteria use up oxygen rotting them. The layering keeps fresh oxygen from the surface away from the bottom water until a storm or the winter mixes it again.
source: Diaz and Rosenberg 2008, Science 321:926-929 (doi:10.1126/science.1156401)

text: Off the mouth of the Changjiang (Yangtze) River, river nutrients feed summer blooms whose sinking remains strip the bottom water of oxygen, under a lid of light river water: in August 1999 the dead zone covered about 13,700 square km.
source: Li et al. 2002, Science in China Series D 45:1137-1146

text: Filamentous cyanobacteria win in warm, calm water poor in nutrients because they make their own nitrogen from the air. Where other algae starve, they have fertiliser to spare.
source: Capone et al. 1997, Science 276:1221-1229

text: Gas vesicles float the filaments up. In calm weather they gather into a scum at the top, catching the light first and shading everyone below: a way to win the race for light.
source: Walsby 1994, Microbiological Reviews 58:94-144

text: Coccolithophores bloom when the water is calm, bright and poor in nutrients, often after the diatoms have used up the silica. They grow slowly, but take up scarce nutrients very efficiently.
source: Tyrrell and Merico 2004, in Coccolithophores: From Molecular Processes to Global Impact, Springer, pp. 75-97

text: The milky turquoise of a coccolithophore bloom is sunlight bouncing off millions of loose chalk plates, shed by the cells as they grow and die.
source: Tyrrell and Merico 2004, in Coccolithophores: From Molecular Processes to Global Impact, Springer, pp. 75-97

text: Coccolithophore blooms often end suddenly when their own virus spreads through the crowded cells: in experiments it caused a quarter to all of the deaths as blooms collapsed.
source: Bratbak, Egge and Heldal 1993, Marine Ecology Progress Series 93:39-48

text: Cryptophytes carry phycobilins, red and blue pigments that catch the green light chlorophyll misses. That lets them grow in dim water beneath a bloom or deeper down, where others go hungry for light.
source: Falkowski and Raven 2007, Aquatic Photosynthesis, Princeton University Press

text: The tiny cyanobacteria win when nutrients are scarce: the smaller a cell, the more surface it has for its volume, so they soak up the last traces of nutrients better than anyone.
source: Partensky, Hess and Vaulot 1999, Microbiology and Molecular Biology Reviews 63:106-127

text: Green flagellates are small and can swim, following the light by day and the nutrients at night. When the water calms and the diatoms run short of silica, they are ready to take over.
source: Reynolds 2006, The Ecology of Phytoplankton, Cambridge University Press

text: When one kind of cell crowds the water, its viruses spread fastest, because the hosts are close together. This kill-the-winner effect cuts blooms down and leaves room for rarer species.
source: Thingstad 2000, Limnology and Oceanography 45:1320-1328

text: Grazers multiply more slowly than algae, so a bloom outruns them at first. When their numbers catch up they eat it down: that lag is why blooms rise and crash.
source: Behrenfeld and Boss 2014, Annual Review of Marine Science 6:167-194

text: River water is fresh, so it floats on the salty sea as a lens. The lens resists the wind's mixing, while the nutrients it carries feed the cells living in it.
source: Simpson and Sharples 2012, Introduction to the Physical and Biological Oceanography of Shelf Seas, Cambridge University Press

text: A strong wind can drive deep water up toward the surface. It is cold and rich in nutrients, so the sunlit water it reaches often greens with a bloom soon after.
source: Mann and Lazier 2006, Dynamics of Marine Ecosystems, Blackwell

text: Spring tides, at new and full moon, run fastest and stir the water from the seabed up. They lift mud and settled particles back into the water and break up the layering near the bottom.
source: Simpson and Sharples 2012, Introduction to the Physical and Biological Oceanography of Shelf Seas, Cambridge University Press

text: Resting cysts wait in the mud of the seabed. They wake only where there is oxygen, so a dead zone keeps them asleep, and the seed bank on the floor outlasts the bad times.
source: Anderson, Taylor and Armbrust 1987, Limnology and Oceanography 32:340-351

text: Diatoms are heavy with glass and cannot swim. They rely on mixing to keep them in the light, which is why they do best in stirred water and sink out when it calms.
source: Smayda 1970, Oceanography and Marine Biology Annual Review 8:353-414

text: Many centric diatoms make resting spores when nutrients run out at the end of a bloom. The spores sink, wait, and seed the next bloom when mixing brings them back up.
source: McQuoid and Hobson 1996, Journal of Phycology 32:889-902

text: Linked into a chain, diatoms are too big for the smallest grazers to swallow: a refuge in size, though a fish or a salp swallows a chain just as easily as a single cell.
source: Smetacek 1999, Protist 150:25-32

text: Long, thin cells sink more slowly than round ones of the same volume, because their shape drags through the water. Linking into colonies slows them further.
source: Padisak, Soroczki-Pinter and Rezner 2003, Hydrobiologia 500:243-257

text: Alexandrium grows slowly, so it cannot win by speed. It wins by poisoning its grazers, by swimming in calm water, and by waiting out the bad months as a cyst.
source: Smayda 1997, Limnology and Oceanography 42:1137-1153

text: Dinophysis cannot make chloroplasts of its own. It feeds on a ciliate that has itself eaten cryptophytes and keeps their chloroplasts working, so it grows only where its prey thrives.
source: Park et al. 2006, Aquatic Microbial Ecology 45:101-106

text: Tripos has long horns that drag through the water like a parachute, slowing its sinking, so it can stay in the calm, sunlit upper water of summer with little effort.
source: Padisak, Soroczki-Pinter and Rezner 2003, Hydrobiologia 500:243-257

text: Prorocentrum thrives in coastal water enriched by rivers and land, and its blooms are spreading as coasts receive more nutrients.
source: Heil, Glibert and Fan 2005, Harmful Algae 4:449-470

text: Small cells win when nutrients are scarce, because the smaller the cell, the more surface it has for its volume to take nutrients in. Big cells do better in dim water, where they burn their stores more slowly.
source: Litchman and Klausmeier 2008, Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution and Systematics 39:615-639

text: Making chalk plates costs a coccolithophore energy. Their main payoff may be armour: plates seem to make the cells harder for grazers to eat.
source: Monteiro et al. 2016, Science Advances 2:e1501822

text: Cryptophytes have no armour and are favourite food for grazers. What keeps them going is light: they grow in dim water other algae cannot use.
source: Reynolds 2006, The Ecology of Phytoplankton, Cambridge University Press

text: Two cousins share the water by depth: Synechococcus, pink with phycoerythrin, likes bright surface water, while Prochlorococcus, the smallest photosynthetic cell known, is tuned to dim light deeper down.
source: Partensky, Hess and Vaulot 1999, Microbiology and Molecular Biology Reviews 63:106-127

text: Filamentous cyanobacteria need warm water, above about 20 degrees, which is why they bloom in summer and fade away in winter.
source: Capone et al. 1997, Science 276:1221-1229

text: Light fades fast with depth: in this coastal sea only about 1% of the sunlight reaches the 60 m floor. Every cell is caught between light from above and nutrients from below.
source: Kirk 2011, Light and Photosynthesis in Aquatic Ecosystems, Cambridge University Press

text: Warm water holds less oxygen, and bacteria rot dead cells faster when it is warm, so dead zones are a late-summer problem.
source: Diaz and Rosenberg 2008, Science 321:926-929 (doi:10.1126/science.1156401)

text: Jellyfish blooms are tied to warm water: warmth speeds their growth and the budding of young jellies, so they swarm most in summer.
source: Purcell 2005, Journal of the Marine Biological Association of the UK 85:461-476
